entries.subject: Use abbreviations to speed up the NTT/INTT proofs (#325)
entries.message:
Use abbreviations to speed up the NTT/INTT proofs (#325)

This makes some changes to the NTT proofs and the underlying
infrastructure, in order to use abbreviations for large subterms. This
improves the runtimes of the x86 NTT/INTT proofs by a factor of
between 1.6 and 4.3 on my test machine, though the approach is
simple-minded and could probably be significantly improved. The two
main new functions used are:

 - ASM_CONGBOUND_RULE is a generalization of GEN_CONGBOUND_RULE to take
   an arbitrary environment of congruence+bound assumptions. This is more
   or less just exposing the internal function "rule" from GEN_CONGBOUND_RULE
   at the top level.

 - SIMD_SIMPLIFY_ABBREV_TAC is a variant of SIMD_SIMPLIFY_TAC that also
   introduces abbreviations for relevant subterms.

The overall structure of the proofs is similar, though in cases with
additional ad-hoc simplifications, steps need to be taken to apply them
also to the abbreviation assumptions.
entries.reason: Speeds x86 NTT/INTT HOL proofs through abbreviations.

entries.subject: Remove separate almost-Montgomery functions for P-256 and P-384
entries.message:
Remove separate almost-Montgomery functions for P-256 and P-384

The almost-Montgomery multiplications and squarings, where full
modular reduction is not guaranteed, do not seem to offer enough
(or in many cases any) performance advantage at the small sizes
of P-256 and P-384, in contrast to larger RSA-sized operations.
These separate functions have been completely deleted, but the
proofs of the "full" Montgomery operations for the NIST primes
(bignum_montmul_p256 etc.) have been augmented with variants
showing that they also work as almost-Montgomery functions. That
is, even without assumptions on the input ranges beyond those
implicit in the native sizes, the appropriate congruence is
guaranteed. It would perhaps be more elegant to put both of these
statements in the same proof, since the current change involves
some duplication of the proof scripts.

entries.subject: AArch64/x86-64: Add persistent cosimulation protocol
entries.message:
AArch64/x86-64: Add persistent cosimulation protocol

Instruction cosimulation checks the HOL Light architecture model against
an external executor. A HOL worker generates an encoded instruction and
input state, sends them to the executor, and compares its output with
the model's result. Each worker currently executes one case through a
shell command:

```text
HOL worker -> temporary output file
           -> armsimulate/x86simulate
              -> preprocess -> assemble -> link -> execute
           -> parse the output file
```

The HOL-side drivers are `arm/proofs/simulator.ml` and
`x86/proofs/simulator.ml`. They generate the instruction and state,
start the executor, and compare its result with the HOL model. The
shared protocol client is implemented in `common/cosim.ml`.

The command-line simulators rebuild and start a temporary executable for
every case. The HOL drivers are also tied to shell argument quoting and
temporary output-file parsing. This repeats process and build startup
costs, and makes it difficult to substitute an emulator or another
instruction-execution transport.

Define version 1 of a line protocol over standard input and output:

```text
HOL worker <-> armsimulate-persistent/x86simulate-persistent
                         -> armsimulate/x86simulate
                            -> preprocess -> assemble -> link -> execute
```

The new wrappers keep the protocol connection open, translate each
request into the legacy command-line form, validate the returned state,
and report `OK`, `TRAP`, or `ERROR`. `READY` identifies the protocol,
architecture, and state size; `QUIT` ends the session.

Each `simulator.ml` selects a default executor command and an
environment variable that can replace it:

```text
S2N_BIGNUM_AARCH64_EXECUTOR
S2N_BIGNUM_X86_64_EXECUTOR
```

The override is a complete shell command, so it can add an emulator
prefix or select another protocol-speaking backend.

This separates case generation from instruction execution and provides
a transport boundary for emulators or other backends. Each request
still follows the historical per-case build path; reusing a compiled
runner is left to a later change.

Signed-off-by: Hanno Becker <beckphan@amazon.co.uk>
entries.reason: Keeps the cosimulation protocol process alive to avoid repeated startup costs.

entries.subject: Use native OCaml compiler to build & run proofs
entries.message:
Use native OCaml compiler to build & run proofs

This patch compiles proofs using native OCaml compiler, and updates
`make proofs` to run the newly created `*.native` executable files.

The new `tools/build-proof.sh` script builds a specific `.ml` proof file.
It inlines all loads/needs in the `.ml` file using HOL Light's
`inline_load.ml`.
Then, it collects all specifications in the original `.ml` file using already existing
`tools/collect-specs.sh`, and adds a print statement at the end of the
file, to make its standard output pass the proof checker script.
It also adds timer and prints the running time of the proof.
Then it is compiled with `ocamlopt.byte`.

Building all proofs can be done with `make build_proofs`. This uses a
lot of memory, so compared to the previous version `-j` number given to
`make` must be reduced.

This also makes the prerequisite lists tidier using the '*.native'
items. Each '.native' file is considered as depending on the '.o' file.
entries.reason: Builds and runs proofs with native OCaml to reduce proof runtime.

entries.subject: Add ARM NEON instructions BIF and REV32 (vector) (#406)
entries.message:
Add ARM NEON instructions BIF and REV32 (vector) (#406)

* Add ARM NEON instructions BIF and REV32 (vector)

Add decode patterns, semantic definitions, and simulator entries for:
- BIF (Bitwise Insert if False): complement of BIT, inserts source
  bits where mask is 0. Supports 64-bit and 128-bit datasize.
- REV32 (vector): reverses byte/halfword order within each 32-bit
  element. Supports esize=8 and esize=16, Q=1 (128-bit) only.

These are needed for verification of the AES-GCM optimised implementation.

Tested: focused sematest with 13,413 random instances (4 processes),
0 failures. Both instructions match hardware cosimulation on AArch64.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Fix alphabetical order: arm_BIF before arm_BIT in ARM_OPERATION_CLAUSES

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Address jargh's suggestion: simplify arm_REV32_VEC using word_reversefields

Replace the explicit word_join/word_subword construction in arm_REV32_VEC
with the word library's word_reversefields, giving a clearer and simpler
implementation. Validated by cosimulating the REV32 instruction against
hardware (600 random reg-states, 0 failures), covering both valid element
sizes (esize=8 byte-reverse, esize=16 halfword swap) and confirming size=10/11
encodings remain UNDEFINED.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entries.subject: Add basic secp256k1 point operations
entries.message:
Add basic secp256k1 point operations

A point doubling function, point addition function, and point mixed
addition function for the secp256k1 curve, all using Jacobian
coordinates with input nondegeneracy assumed. The addition and
mixed addition functions offer only marginal efficiency gains over
just calling a sequence of basic field operations, but the doubling
has some beneficial mathematically equivalent short-cutting of the
intermediate modular reductions.
entries.reason: Adds point doubling with shorter intermediate modular reductions.

Use rodata section for all ARM code with constant data (#267)

the constant tables.

* Fix up code copies inside proofs for new rodata-based code

The first step in fixing up the proofs.

This does an initial fixup of the auxiliary lemmas before the
main proofs.

* More rodata fixup for Edwards scalar mul base proofs

* Tweak table proofs in Edwards base multiplications

Some mistaken cut-and-paste from curve25519 versions, but the
two base cases are different and the offset is different.

* More misc Edwards rodata fixups

* Add ARM adrp instruction to allowed instruction list

* Add adrp pattern to skipped instructions for simulator

* Improve SUBROUTINE_SIM_TAC tactics for subroutines with rodata

The existing [ARM|X86]_SUBROUTINE_SIM_TAC did not work satisfactorily
when the subroutine contained rodata (as is already allowed for ARM
and will be for x86 soon). Among other problems, it did not handle
the minor syntactic differences between ways of expressing relative

more rodata parameters than the subroutine. These changes make the
situation much more robust.

By enclosing some offset expressions like 96+5*16 in parentheses.

entries.subject: Avoid access to stack pointer + negative offset in p384_montjadd
entries.message:
Avoid access to stack pointer + negative offset in p384_montjadd

This is a patch that fixes p384_montjadd and p384_montjscalarmul (which
has p384_montjadd inlined) to avoid memory access to stack pointer +
negative offset in the middle of the function.
This is because when a process is interrupted, in principle, context
switching to a handler may overwrite data under the stack pointer:
https://forum.osdev.org/viewtopic.php?t=21720
This also caused valgrind from AWS-LC side to fail.

This is porting the patch of @dkostic:
https://github.com/aws/aws-lc/pull/2036/commits/65808f80b26171e2d66347b84f99c1acb26efee6
.. and also updates the proof according to it.
Also, this adds valgrind to the test so that it can print such cases.

entries.subject: Add ML-KEM forward and inverse NTT for ARM
entries.message:
Add ML-KEM forward and inverse NTT for ARM

This sets up ARM code for the forward and inverse number-theoretic
transforms that are used in ML-KEM

  https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/fips/nist.fips.203.pdf

These efficient ARM implementations are taken, with minor
modifications, from the SLOTHY-generated machine code here:

  https://github.com/pq-code-package/mlkem-native

They are then formally verified using the s2n-bignum infrastructure.

This is ARM-only so far; we have not yet set up x86 equivalents.

entries.subject: Arm: Add four-register LD1 and ST1 (#436)
entries.message:
Arm: Add four-register LD1 and ST1 (#436)

Model the AArch64 multiple-structure forms that load or store four
consecutive SIMD registers. Support 64- and 128-bit register lists with
no offset, post-immediate writeback, or post-register writeback.

Treat each operation as a contiguous little-endian transfer, including
register-list wraparound and the full memory event span. Register the
decoder and load/store clauses, and add a bounded memory generator so
the new forms are checked against hardware.

These forms are needed by the x265 AArch64 proof work.

entries.subject: Add first SM2 field operations, addition and subtraction
entries.message:
Add first SM2 field operations, addition and subtraction

This begins the support of the SM2 curve from the "Commercial
Cryptography" standard (see GM/T 0003-2012 and ISO/IEC 14888). The
first two functions are addition and subtraction modulo the field
characteristic p_sm2 = 2^256 - 2^224 - 2^96 + 2^64 - 1.

These are highly analogous to P-256 functions, and in fact the ARM
bignum_add_p256 is tweaked here so that both adopt the same style,
using subtraction of the characteristic followed by selection instead
of masked resubtraction; this is slightly shorter and faster at the
expense of using more registers.

entries.subject: Make symbolic simulation for equiv checking infer output of loads
entries.message:
Make symbolic simulation for equiv checking infer output of loads

This patch updates symbolic simulation tactics for equivalence checking to infer the output of memory loads from assumptions if there is no directly matching equality.

For example, if there is an assumption `read (memory :> bytes (ptr,8*n)) = a` but nothing about `read (memory :> bytes64 (word_add (ptr,8*k)))`, it tries to construct its output as `bigdigit a k` using `SIMPLE_ARITH_TAC`. This helps remove boilerplate codes in proofs that manually construct all equalities between 64-bit and 128-bit memory reads at known locations, which typically looked like:
```
REPEAT (FIRST_X_ASSUM BIGNUM_EXPAND_AND_DIGITIZE_TAC) THEN
ASM_PROPAGATE_DIGIT_EQS_FROM_EXPANDED_BIGNUM_TAC THEN
(* necessary to run ldr qs *)
COMBINE_READ_BYTES64_PAIRS_TAC THEN
```

This also reduces the sizes of assumptions, which may affect positive results to proof checking times, but in fact caused slowdown to larger equivalence checking tactics such as p256/p384's point operations, hence they are manually written.

The main tactics are `MK_MEMORY_READ_EQ_BIGDIGIT_CONV` and `DIGITIZE_MEMORY_READS_TAC`.
They construct equations involving the unseen memory reads and `bigdigit`. They are passed to `ARM_N_STEP_TAC` (the `ARM_STEP'_TAC` in the past; this renaming will be explained below), which are called 'auxiliary memory read equations, and they are either `ASSUME_TAC`ed or passed to the caller separately from other normal equations describing the actual outputs of a simulated instruction.

On top of these updates, I also added a few utility functions like `get_input_output_regs` which gets the input and output register from a basic block. These will be used in my future patches.

entries.subject: Add SIMD multiplication by a single element to the ARM model
entries.message:
Add SIMD multiplication by a single element to the ARM model

This allows a variant of SIMD multiplication "by element", i.e.
multiplying each lane of the first source operand by the *same*
single lane of the second source operand.

To express this conveniently, we introduce "lane" components
LANE_B, LANE_H, LANE_S and LANE_D, so for example the ARM
assembler syntax "v2.h[1]" corresponds to "Q2 :> LANE_H 1"
in the abstract syntax. These lane components include appropriate
duplication to an equivalent SIMD argument, so that the core
operation is expressed uniformly for the "by element" and
"vector" variants.

entries.subject: Adopt enhanced WORD_SIMPLE_SUBWORD_CONV from latest HOL Light (#299)
entries.message:
Adopt enhanced WORD_SIMPLE_SUBWORD_CONV from latest HOL Light (#299)

This bumps the assumed HOL Light commit to update the inherited
conversion WORD_SIMPLE_SUBWORD_CONV. This allows some proofs to
be slightly simplified, although in the proofs of the ARM
Lenngren-style X25519, there is some additional compensation
needed because it now simplifies too much.

We also now take advantage of the fix to the type of usimd16 in HOL Light to
use it in PMOVMSKB (previously a usimd2+usimd8 workaround was used).

entries.subject: Slightly improve x86 P-256 and P-384 Montgomery operations
entries.message:
Slightly improve x86 P-256 and P-384 Montgomery operations

This commit makes various minor local improvements such as the use of
32-bit operations where possible (which generally reduces code size),
and generates some big constants avoiding the use of 64-bit immediate
moves. The Montgomery multiplies also do some of the top parts of
carry chains in a slightly more efficient way; this is the only case
where the actual dataflow changes, and even so the same proofs still
work modulo the instruction offsets and code size changes. Code size
is reduced for sure, and there seems to be some slight (maybe 1-3%?)
efficiency gain on both Xeon and EPYC. This commit also makes a couple
of tweaks to simulation in order to handle 32-bit ADC more nicely and
to trivialize the zero-extension of single-bit values "word(bitval b)".
entries.reason: Reduces code size and carry-chain work in P-256/P-384 Montgomery operations.

entries.subject: Consistently use upper case for constants
entries.message:
Consistently use upper case for constants

Numeric constants from "#define" and assembler-level values
from ".set" are now always uppercase. This makes it easier to parse
the assembler files in a context-free way for scripting purposes.
This does not change the text section of any object file and hence
does not require proof changes. However the .set directives do
add a symbol to the symbol table, and those have changed in the
following from "i" to "I":

        arm/fastmul/bignum_kmul_16_32.o
        arm/fastmul/bignum_kmul_32_64.o
        arm/fastmul/bignum_ksqr_16_32.o
        arm/fastmul/bignum_ksqr_32_64.o

entries.subject: Slightly optimize curve25519 field multiplication and squaring
entries.message:
Slightly optimize curve25519 field multiplication and squaring

Both bignum_mul_p25519 and bignum_sqr_p25519 in effect reduce
a double-length 2^256 * h + l to congruent 38 * h + l and then
further reduce based on a quotient estimate from the latter.
The new versions slightly reduce dependent latencies and/or
number of instructions by forming the quotient estimate before
the full computation of 38 * h + l and feeding the subsequent
correction in earlier as a result.
entries.reason: Reduces dependent latency and instruction count in curve25519 multiplication and squaring.

entries.subject: Enable x86 indirect branch tracking in code and proofs (#203)
entries.message:
Enable x86 indirect branch tracking in code and proofs (#203)

* x86: add script for adding endbr{32,64} instructions

* Implement CET for amd64

* Sync AT&T syntax files

* Add ENDBR64 to x86 model

This is intended to support the insertion of ENDBR64 into the x86
code to support indirect branch tracking (IBT), part of CET
(control-flow enforcement technology).

The actual semantics assumed is simply a NOP; on machines without
CET enabled, including older machines from before the feature
existed, this is indeed how it behaves. We do not attempt to model
the restrictions that are imposed when CET is enabled, and such
restrictions arguably belong on the indirect branches themselves, of
which there are none in s2n-bignum itself.

For more discussion see

  https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56905811/what-does-the-endbr64-instruction-actually-do

* Enable IBT by default in the code

This makes the code compile with IBT unless explicitly flagged
otherwise in the compiler options, hence inserting one initial
ENDBR64 instruction at the main entry point for each function.

The copy of the code given in each "define_assert_from_elf" is
also updated correspondingly.

So far, the proofs are not updated, though the

* Re-derive non-IBT version of code and restore proofs

This uses the function define_trimmed that trims away the first 4
bytes of the code (expected to be ENDBR64) and makes a definition
matching the non-IBT original, hence restoring the proofs.

* Use symbolic lengths for most x86 toplevel correctness theorems

This switches most xxx_SUBROUTINE_CORRECT statements to use
explicit "LENGTH code" hypotheses in place of explicit numbers.
The main unchanged ones are those with data in the text section
as well.

* Add IBT variants of x86 toplevel correctness statements

Every xxx_SUBROUTINE_CORRECT result, both standard and Windows ABI,
now has a variant xxx_IBT_SUBROUTINE_CORRECT in the file, with a
proof that mostly works automatically via the new ADD_IBT_RULE,
corresponding to the case where the code is prefixed by ENDBR64.
This rule fails to handle the cases with data in the text section;
this occurs in these proofs that will need fixing next:

        edwards25519_scalarmuldouble_alt.ml
        edwards25519_scalarmuldouble.ml
        edwards25519_scalarmulbase_alt.ml
        edwards25519_scalarmulbase.ml
        curve25519_x25519base_alt.ml
        curve25519_x25519base.ml

* Fix remaining IBT proof breaks

This is done by making ADD_IBT_RULE a little more robust so that it
handles the case of appended code and data tables, and also modifies
explicit code length numbers as well as symbolic lengths.

* Invert naming conventions for x86 Windows and IBT versions

This switches around the naming conventions in correctness theorems
and machine code definitions:

 * Instead of the IBT forms of correctness theorems having their names
   flagged with _IBT, that is now the default and the others are
   labelled explicitly as _NOIBT

 * The WINDOWS_ modifier is used as a suffix not a prefix in correctness
   statements, and likewise for windows_ in the machine code definitions.

 * The full machine code with ENDBR64 has a name ending _mc and the
   trimmed form without ENDBR64 has a name ending _tmc (t for trimmed).

* Use platform CET header where possible

The explicit ENDBR64 definition is now only used if the platform is
not already enabling CET. This improvement was suggested by lgv5 in
the discussion at https://github.com/awslabs/s2n-bignum/pull/173

* Expand ENDBR64 explanatory comment, fix whitespace

Where "fix whitespace" means both of the following:

  (1) remove all trailing spaces
  (2) expand all tabs to spaces, except in Makefiles and tools.

* Install libpcre2-dev in the CI codebuild
